categories.name: HR Questions
categories.description: General questions about you, your motivation and your fit with the company.
tips: Research the company's products, values and recent news before the interview.
Keep answers to about 1–2 minutes and stay positive.
Prepare two or three questions to ask the interviewer at the end.

questions.question: Tell me about yourself.
questions.tip: Use a present–past–future structure and connect it to the role.
questions.sampleAnswer: I'm a final-year Computer Science student focusing on mobile development. Over the last two years I've built several iOS apps for university projects, including a job tracker using SwiftUI and Firebase. I also worked as a lab teaching assistant, which improved my communication skills. Now I'm looking for an internship where I can contribute to real products and keep learning from experienced engineers.
keyPoints: Why you are interested in this role

questions.question: Why do you want to work for our company?
questions.tip: Mention something specific about the company, not just the salary or location.
questions.sampleAnswer: I've used your app regularly and I like how simple the experience is. I also read about your engineering team's focus on mobile performance, which matches what I enjoy working on. I believe I can learn a lot here and contribute with my SwiftUI experience.
keyPoints: A specific product, value or achievement of the company
How it connects to your interests

questions.question: What are your strengths?
questions.tip: Pick strengths that matter for the job and prove each one with an example.
questions.sampleAnswer: One of my strengths is breaking down large problems. In my last semester project I split a big app into small modules with clear tasks, and we finished a week early. I'm also a quick learner: I learned Firebase in two weeks to add cloud sync to a project.

questions.question: What is your biggest weakness?
questions.tip: Choose a real but non-critical weakness and show how you are improving.
questions.sampleAnswer: I sometimes spend too long polishing details. I've started time-boxing tasks and asking for feedback earlier, which helps me deliver on time while keeping good quality.

questions.question: Where do you see yourself in five years?
questions.tip: Show ambition that fits the company's growth path.
questions.sampleAnswer: I see myself as a strong mobile engineer who owns features end to end and mentors newer developers. I'd like to grow inside a team where I can take on more responsibility over time.
keyPoints: Link to the role and company

questions.question: What are your salary expectations?
questions.tip: Research typical ranges first and give a range rather than a single number.
questions.sampleAnswer: Based on my research for similar roles in this city, I'm expecting something in the range of X to Y. I'm flexible, and learning opportunities are also very important to me.

categories.name: Behavioral Questions
categories.description: Questions about how you acted in real situations. Use the STAR method.
tips: Use STAR: Situation, Task, Action, Result.
Focus on what YOU did, even in team projects.
Prepare 4–5 stories you can adapt to different questions.

questions.question: Tell me about a time you worked in a team.
questions.tip: Highlight communication and your specific role.
questions.sampleAnswer: In our database course project (Situation), our team of four had to design a library system (Task). I set up a shared task board and weekly meetings, and I designed the schema (Action). We submitted on time and got one of the highest grades in the class (Result).

questions.question: Describe a conflict with a teammate and how you handled it.
questions.tip: Stay neutral, never blame, and show a calm resolution.
questions.sampleAnswer: Two teammates disagreed about which framework to use. I suggested we list the requirements and compare both options against them. We picked one together, and the person whose idea wasn't chosen led the testing part, so everyone stayed involved.

questions.question: Tell me about a time you failed.
questions.tip: Choose a real failure and focus on what you learned.
questions.sampleAnswer: In my first hackathon I tried to build too many features and our demo crashed. I learned to agree on a minimum working version first. In the next hackathon we delivered a stable demo and placed in the top five.
keyPoints: How you applied the lesson later

questions.question: Describe a time you had to meet a tight deadline.
questions.tip: Show planning and prioritization.
questions.sampleAnswer: Two assignments and a lab exam fell in the same week. I listed tasks by deadline and effort, finished the smaller assignment first and used short focused sessions for the bigger one. I submitted both on time and did well in the exam.

questions.question: Give an example of when you showed leadership.
questions.tip: Leadership does not require a title; show initiative.
questions.sampleAnswer: When our project group lost momentum, I proposed splitting the work into weekly milestones and offered to coordinate. I checked in with each member and helped one teammate who was stuck. The project was completed and the professor praised our organization.

categories.name: Technical Questions
categories.description: Programming, iOS and computer science fundamentals.
tips: Think out loud so the interviewer can follow your reasoning.
Ask clarifying questions before writing code.
Mention time and space complexity when discussing solutions.

questions.question: What is the difference between a struct and a class in Swift?
questions.tip: Focus on value vs reference semantics.
questions.sampleAnswer: Structs are value types: when you assign or pass them, a copy is made. Classes are reference types: variables share the same instance. Classes also support inheritance and deinitializers. SwiftUI prefers structs for views and models because copies are predictable.

questions.question: Explain @State, @Binding and @ObservedObject in SwiftUI.
questions.tip: Explain who owns the data in each case.
questions.sampleAnswer: @State stores simple data owned by a view. @Binding gives a child view read-write access to state owned by a parent. @ObservedObject watches an external ObservableObject passed in from outside, while @StateObject creates and owns one so it survives view updates.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of searching in a balanced binary search tree?
questions.tip: Relate the answer to the height of the tree.
questions.sampleAnswer: Searching a balanced BST is O(log n) because each comparison removes about half of the remaining nodes. In an unbalanced tree it can degrade to O(n).
keyPoints: O(log n) average for balanced trees

questions.question: How would you reverse a linked list?
questions.tip: Draw the pointers before coding.
questions.sampleAnswer: I would use three pointers: previous, current and next. While current is not nil, I save next, point current.next to previous, then move previous and current one step forward. At the end, previous is the new head. This is O(n) time and O(1) space.
keyPoints: Edge cases: empty or single node

questions.question: What is the difference between SQL and NoSQL databases?
questions.tip: Give an example of when you would choose each.
questions.sampleAnswer: SQL databases store data in tables with a fixed schema and support joins and strong consistency. NoSQL databases like Firestore store flexible documents and scale easily. I used Firestore in CareerTrack because each user's data is naturally a set of documents.

questions.question: Explain what happens when you type a URL into a browser.
questions.tip: Go step by step from DNS to rendering.
questions.sampleAnswer: The browser resolves the domain with DNS, opens a TCP connection (and TLS for HTTPS), sends an HTTP request, and the server returns a response. The browser then parses HTML, loads CSS, JavaScript and images, and renders the page.

categories.name: Internship Questions
categories.description: Questions commonly asked to students applying for internships.
tips: Talk about university projects as real experience.
Show eagerness to learn and accept feedback.
Know your own CV well; every line can become a question.

questions.question: Why are you interested in this internship?
questions.tip: Connect the internship to your studies and career goals.
questions.sampleAnswer: This internship lets me apply what I learned in mobile computing to a real product. I want to learn how professional teams review code and release apps, and your team works on exactly the kind of apps I want to build.

questions.question: Tell me about a project you are proud of.
questions.tip: Explain the problem, your role, the technology and the result.
questions.sampleAnswer: I'm proud of CareerTrack, an iOS app to manage job applications. I built it with SwiftUI and Firebase, including authentication, cloud storage, reminders and analytics. It taught me how to organize code with view models and services.

questions.question: How do you handle feedback or criticism?
questions.tip: Show that you see feedback as a way to improve.
questions.sampleAnswer: I try to listen fully, ask questions to understand, and then act on it. When my lab instructor said my code lacked comments, I started writing short explanations for complex logic, and my next submissions were easier to review.

questions.question: How do you balance studies with other responsibilities?
questions.tip: Show organization and realistic planning.
questions.sampleAnswer: I use a weekly planner and block time for classes, assignments and my teaching assistant work. I start large tasks early and review my plan every Sunday.

questions.question: What do you want to learn during this internship?
questions.tip: Be specific: tools, processes and soft skills.
questions.sampleAnswer: I want to learn how to write production-quality code, use code review and testing properly, and work in an agile team. I'd also like to improve my communication with designers and product managers.
